newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Ringgit sinks to 39-mth low on fresh selling.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ringgit sinks to 39-mth low on fresh selling.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit sank more than 1.5 percent late on Friday to a 39-month low against the dollar after Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said he was happy with the currency's level.
At 1300 GMT, the ringgit was at 2.6830/60 to one dollar, its lowest level since May 5, 1994. The currency has fallen around 7.4 percent since a month ago.
"There's big buying of dollar/Malay out of London. They are pushing the dollar higher," said a U.S. bank dealer in London.
The ringgit has been under a speculative attack along with other Southeast Asian currencies for over a month.
Dealers said Mahathir's remark gave players a further excuse to buy up dollars.
Mahathir told reporters on Friday the ringgit's fall of about five percent against the dollar was not much "if compared with the deutschemark which has fallen by 17 percent".

Around 0900 GMT, Bank Negara, the central bank, had intervened in the market to defend the ringgit as the currency faced a fresh round of speculative selling. The central bank sold the dollar for ringgit through an agent bank at 2.6500/10, dealers said.
Bank Negara spent $2.0-3.0 billion of its reserves in June to defend the ringgit from speculative attack.
Analysts said the ringgit was expected to remain under pressure on fears of possible overheating in the economy.
They said the concern about the economy followed Malaysia's surprisingly high loans and monetary growth figures for June, despite steps by the central bank to curb them.
Bank Negara announced on Wednesday that broad money supply, or M3, grew by 21.9 percent year-on-year in June against 20.3 percent in May and 22.9 percent in the same month last year.
Loans growth in June rose to an annualised 30 percent from 29.5 percent at the end of May.

"The numbers helped fuse a change in views on Malaysia," said Philip Wee, regional treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore. "The focus has shifted to overheating of the economy. This will not help the ringgit which will remain under pressure."
Analysts and dealers said the ringgit could weaken to 2.70 a dollar in the near term.
"I don't think the Malaysian authorities can do much about it because these are not just speculative flows. There are actual capital outflows as well," said a Singapore dealer.
An unexpectedly large trade deficit for June and a weak stock market added fresh pressure on the beleaguered ringgit.
Malaysia on Monday reported a trade deficit of 2.8 billion ringgit ($1.1 billion) for June after a surplus of 156.2 million ringgit in May.

Capital control measures, introduced by the central bank on Sunday to cool speculation in the ringgit and push down interest rates, have rattled the stock market, driving down the benchmark index more than seven percent this week.
Bank Negara ordered local banks to limit non-trade related currency swaps to $2.0 million with each overseas customer, in an attempt to reduce foreigners access to ringgit.
But analysts said the curbs, which followed stinging verbal attacks on speculators by Mahathir, have not helped the ringgit much and are unlikely to prevent further gains in the dollar.
They said most funds were comfortably hedged for their ringgit requirements in the forward swaps market before the restrictions were imposed.
"The focus has now moved from the region to Malaysia due to its domestic factors," said Wee of Standard Chartered Bank.
"The economy is growing at a stronger rate than what the authorities want to see, and this is worrisome," he said.
